analysis.one_liner: Requires phone, cable, satellite, and internet providers to automatically credit customers for service outages.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 18, 2026 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee; it has no cosponsors and no committee action yet, with Congress in session through January 3, 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require telephone, cable, satellite TV, and internet providers with more than 5,000 customers to automatically credit customers one-thirtieth of the monthly rate for each day their service is out for four hours or more. Customers who cancel service after an outage could receive any leftover credit as a check, a no-fee prepaid card, or an electronic transfer within 30 days. It also directs the FCC and FTC to write rules improving customer service, call-record access, missed appointments, and equipment returns, and requires broadband providers to report outages during disasters.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and small businesses that pay monthly bills to telephone, cable, satellite, and internet companies. Today, getting a credit for an outage usually requires calling and negotiating with the provider; this bill would make the credit automatic, including for people with disabilities or without transportation who face extra burdens when service fails or equipment must be returned.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households paying cable, phone, and internet bills

how_it_helps.text: Providers must automatically credit one-thirtieth of the monthly rate for each day a service is unavailable or out for four hours or more, with no request from the customer required [S2].
Customers who terminate service can receive any credit exceeding their bill within 30 days as a check, a no-fee prepaid debit card, or an electronic transfer, at their choice [S2].

The FCC must write rules within 18 months extending cable customer-service standards to satellite, voice, and broadband service, requiring providers to keep call recordings for at least a year and give them to customers on request, and barring fees to speak with a live representative; the FTC must set standards for missed service appointments and ease equipment-return burdens for people with disabilities or without cars [S2].
The rules apply to providers with more than 5,000 customers, covering the major wireless carriers, cable and satellite companies, and broadband providers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Telephone, cable, satellite, and broadband companies, which would give up billing revenue during outages and bear the cost of automatic credits, refund disbursements, longer call recordings, and improved customer-service operations. Those costs would ultimately come from the same companies' margins; customers never get more than their own monthly rate back.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large telecom, cable, and satellite providers

drawbacks.text: The credit is small by design: one-thirtieth of the monthly rate per day equals one full day's rate, and providers are exempt if a refund would cost more to disburse than it is worth, so the relief for a customer is limited to the service price and never covers damages like lost wages or spoiled food [S2].

Outages during announced pre-planned maintenance do not count, and enforcement depends entirely on FCC rulemaking within 18 months of enactment, so the protections would not exist until the agency writes detailed rules [S2].

Providers must credit for outages even those outside their direct control, such as weather or power failures on the customer's end of the network, which some would argue is difficult to administer fairly; the bill text does not carve out force-majeure events other than scheduled maintenance [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to customers is real but modest: automatic credits worth one day's rate per outage day and better customer service, at the cost of administrative burden to providers. The strongest criticism is that the remedy is capped at the subscription price, so it does not compensate customers for the wider costs of losing internet or phone service, and that everything hinges on future FCC and FTC rulemaking.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján introduced the bill on May 18, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S4].
No cosponsors had joined the bill as of the provided record [S3].
No markup, hearing, or vote is recorded; the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill is pending with no action beyond referral, telecom, cable, and satellite providers are unaffected for now and keep the status quo in which outage credits are voluntary; customers have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Providers keep the status quo; no outcome yet

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, on which he has served.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or committee action have occurred, and no member besides the sponsor has taken a position in the record, so no partisan split is visible yet.

industries.industry: Telephone, cable, satellite TV, and broadband providers
industries.note: These companies would have to automatically credit a day's rate per outage day, refund leftover credits after cancellation, keep customer-service call recordings for a year, and improve service for missed appointments and equipment returns. Their interest in avoiding automatic refunds runs against customers who currently must request credits case by case.
Providers would need to build outage-detection, automatic-crediting, and call-recording capabilities, creating demand for compliance systems. This is a secondary effect of the bill.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills introduced in the Senate never receive committee action, and this one has been referred without cosponsors or committee activity. Unless the sponsor builds cosponsor support or the Commerce Committee schedules action, the bill is likely to sit in committee until the Congress ends in January 2027.
